title: Whether One Attains Rebirth
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: What is meant by “Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation”?

inline.s: Question: What is meant by “Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation”?
Answer: These two lines come from Master Ouyi’s Essential Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra, which reads:

“Faith, vows, and name-recitation are the essential purport of this sūtra. Faith and vows are the wisdom-practice; name-recitation is the action-practice. Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation. Thus the wisdom-practice serves as the forerunner, and the action-practice as the true cultivation — like eyes and feet moving together.”

In this passage, “faith, vows, and name-recitation are the essential purport of this sūtra” means that these three — faith, vows, and practice (name-recitation) — are inseparable; they are the essential purport of this sūtra, and likewise the essential path of Pure Land practice. “Faith and vows are the wisdom-practice; name-recitation is the action-practice,” and “thus the wisdom-practice serves as the forerunner, and the action-practice as the true cultivation — like eyes and feet moving together” mean: faith and vows are the forerunner, like the eyes; name-recitation is the true cultivation, like the pair of feet. Without eyes one would wander blindly, and without feet one cannot move forward at all. Therefore, seen in the context of “whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation,”

these two lines mean: one who attains rebirth must have faith and vows, and must also have the practice of name-recitation. Those whose practice is deep attain rebirth at a high grade; those whose practice is shallow attain rebirth at a low grade.

Question: That is not right. “Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows” should mean: so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth. Moreover, Master Yinguang praised these two lines highly, because they tell us that the most important condition for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is this: so long as you have true faith and true vows, you will attain rebirth.
Answer:
To interpret “whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows” as “so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth”
involves two problems:

1. If it is understood this way, then “whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation” would mean: so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth; and so long as one has the practice of name-recitation, one attains rebirth (with deep practice, rebirth at a high grade; with shallow practice, rebirth at a low grade). In that case, the first half says that so long as one has faith and vows one attains rebirth, while the second half says that so long as one has the practice of name-recitation one attains rebirth. Then is rebirth attained merely by having faith and vows, or merely by having the practice of name-recitation? Think about it — how could Master Ouyi ever utter such a self-contradictory statement?! Therefore, one must pay particular attention to the difference in meaning between the two terms “quán yóu” (entirely owing to) and “quán píng” (entirely relying on): “quán yóu” expresses a necessary condition (an indispensable condition), while “quán píng” expresses a sufficient condition (this condition alone suffices).

2. In this passage of the Essential Commentary, Master Ouyi states very clearly that faith and vows are the guide (the one who leads the way) and name-recitation is the true cultivation (the one who carries it out). How could it suffice to have only the guide without the true cultivation? Moreover, the Master gives a vivid analogy: faith and vows are like the eyes, and name-recitation is like the feet. For a practitioner to reach the destination (the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss), the eyes must watch the road and the feet must walk (eyes and feet moving together). How could one reach the destination with only eyes to watch the road while the feet never walk? Just as Master Ouyi instructs in the earlier section “Clarifying the Tenet” (míng zōng) of the Essential Commentary:
“The tenet is the essential path of cultivation

. This sūtra takes faith, vows, and name-recitation as the essential tenet of its practice. Without faith, vows cannot be aroused; without vows, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of name-recitation, one’s vows cannot be fulfilled and one’s faith cannot be verified.

Faith means believing in oneself and in others, believing in cause and effect, believing in phenomena and in principle; vows mean renouncing this Sahā world and joyfully seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice means holding fast to the name,
with single-mindedness, without confusion.
(For details, see
Annotations on the Essential Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra
Please note: when Master Ouyi explains faith, vows, and practice in the passage above, he states explicitly:
“Without the wondrous practice of name-recitation, one’s vows cannot be fulfilled and one’s faith cannot be verified.”
Practice means holding fast to the name, with single-mindedness, without confusion.”
He sets forth with perfect clarity the relationship among faith, vows, and practice, and the requirement for practice.
Therefore, when Master Yinguang quotes “
Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation
”, he first makes clear:
With practice but without faith and vows, one cannot attain rebirth; with faith and vows but without practice, one likewise cannot attain rebirth.
When faith, vows, and practice are complete and lacking in nothing, rebirth is assured.
Master Yinguang’s full instruction is:

“Now that you have true faith and earnest vows, you should cultivate the true practice of Buddha-recitation. Take faith and vows as the guide, and Buddha-recitation as the true practice. Faith, vows, and practice — these three are the
essential tenet
of the Buddha-recitation method.
With practice but without faith and vows, one cannot attain rebirth; with faith and vows but without practice, one likewise cannot attain rebirth.
When faith, vows, and practice are complete and lacking in nothing, rebirth is assured.
‘Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation.’”
(Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, “Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou”)
Before quoting “
Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one’s rebirth depends entirely on the depth of one’s name-recitation
”, Master Yinguang had already made it utterly clear:
“When faith, vows, and practice are complete and lacking in nothing, rebirth is assured.”
And Master Yinguang instructed explicitly:
“With faith and vows but without practice, one likewise cannot attain rebirth.”
Where does he ever say that one can attain rebirth merely by having true faith and true vows? What is more, faith and vows without true practice — how could they ever be true faith and true vows?
Moreover, if Master Ouyi had truly held that “one attains rebirth merely by having faith and vows,” why, in the midst of a grave illness at the brink of death, because
“his mind was clear yet his strength was not his own”
did he
“weep and cry out, not knowing what to do
(utterly at a loss)
? And why did he repent of his
“neglect of contemplative practice”
? Why would he hasten to establish a pure-land society and strive diligently in Buddha-recitation in order to seek rebirth? And he further said:
“If I do not urgently spur myself in the pure work
(that is, if I do not urgently and earnestly press on in pure practice)
, how shall I ever escape the wheel of suffering
(how can I forever leave the round of birth and death)
(For details, see
“Vows on Founding a Pure-Land Society During a Grave Illness”
, an essay
The reason Buddha-recitation requires single-mindedness is that “through the pure mind of Buddha-recitation, one evokes birth in the Western Pure Land.”
Master Yinguang said:

“If one’s own mind is not pure, how can one attain rebirth at once? Even a person of grave offenses who attains rebirth by reciting the Buddha’s name ten times does so through the pure mind of Buddha-recitation, which evokes birth in the Western Pure Land.”
(Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, “Answers to Layman Qu Tianxiang’s Twenty-seven Questions”) Master Yinguang also said:
Reciting the Buddha’s name with a scattered mind, one can hardly attain rebirth.
This method can bring the mind back to a single point; reciting with single-mindedness, rebirth is assured.”
(Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, “Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou”)
Therefore, the essential key to ensuring rebirth is:
true faith, earnest vows, and single-mindedness without confusion.

This is also the guiding program of practice for one who recites the Buddha’s name. Because of true faith, one’s vision illumines the scene ahead and sees the goal and the road with perfect clarity; because of earnest vows, one’s power is immensely strong — like a river bursting its banks, overwhelming and impossible to resist. With true faith and earnest vows, one will surely follow the World-Honored One’s earnest teaching to “practice as one is taught,” and thus bring about the wondrous practice of single-mindedness; and with this wondrous practice of single-mindedness one verifies what one has believed and fulfills what one has vowed: “Now that single-mindedness is attained, (at the hour of death) then
inwardly one concentrates right mindfulness, and outwardly one evokes the Buddha’s coming to welcome one
; casting off this present body, one is reborn straightway in that land.” (Master Lianchi, Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra)
[Pèi rán mò zhī néng yù — surging and vast, nothing whatever can withstand it.]

It should be noted that when faith and vows remain only in the mind, they are nothing more than an idea. Faith and vows must be put into practice; only then are they true faith and earnest vows. Therefore, true faith and earnest vows necessarily lead to vigorous practice. Without earnest, diligent Buddha-recitation, how can one verify what one believes? How can one fulfill what one vows? Faith and vows without vigorous practice are merely hollow faith and floating vows. Master Ouyi said:
“The method of Buddha-recitation has nothing else extraordinary about it; only deep faith and
vigorous practice
are essential.”
(Lingfeng Zonglun, Collected Writings of Master Ouyi)
Therefore, concerning the relationship among true faith, earnest vows, and vigorous practice, Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) instructed:
“As for those without faith, let them be set aside for now
(those who do not believe may be left aside without mention)

. Take even those who believe: to believe yet not vow is still not to believe; to vow yet not practice is still not to vow; to practice yet not vigorously is still not to practice. Practice fails to be vigorous because the vow is not earnest; the vow fails to be earnest because the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is hard. If faith is truly genuine, the vow will naturally be earnest; if the vow is truly earnest, practice will naturally be vigorous. With genuine faith and earnest vows, joined to brave and vigorous practice, one is certain to be reborn in the Pure Land, certain to see Amitābha, certain to attain the threefold non-retrogression, and certain to become a Buddha in one final lifetime.”
(The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)
Question: The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life says:

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions who with sincere hearts believe and rejoice, and who wish to be born in my land, should recite my name even ten times and yet not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment — excepting those who commit the five grave offenses or slander the true Dharma.”
Therefore, so long as one has true faith, by reciting the Buddha’s name ten times one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Answer: In the sūtra, “even ten recitations” refers to ten uninterrupted recitations at the hour of death. (For details, see
“The Eighteenth Vow”
Question: The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life says:

“All sentient beings who hear his name, rejoice with faith, and with even a single thought sincerely dedicate the merit, wishing to be born in that land, shall immediately attain rebirth and abide in non-retrogression — excepting those who commit the five grave offenses or slander the true Dharma.”
Therefore, so long as one has true faith, by sincerely dedicating the merit once, one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Answer: In “with even a single thought sincerely dedicate the merit,” the phrase “a single thought” means to make one’s thought single. Thus “even a single thought, sincerely dedicated” means to make one’s thought single-pointed (free of scattered thoughts) and to dedicate it with utmost sincerity — not “to dedicate the merit once.” If one understands it as “dedicate the merit once, and one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss,” does such an understanding hold up? Does it accord with the actual circumstances of rebirth?

In sum, do “so long as one has true faith, reciting the Buddha’s name ten times suffices for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss” and “so long as one has true faith, dedicating the merit sincerely once suffices for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss” accord with how Pure Land practitioners actually attain rebirth? The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life says:

“The path ascending has no end or limit; easy to go there, yet no one goes. That land refuses none, yet beings are drawn along by their own natural karma. Why not cast aside worldly affairs and diligently practice to seek the Way of virtue? One may then gain life immeasurably long, with bliss and longevity without end.”

Does the “true faith” you speak of live up to “Why not cast aside worldly affairs and diligently practice to seek the Way of virtue”? Does it live up to the Buddha’s admonition that follows? The Buddha said:

“I now tell you: because people cling to worldly affairs, they sit here unable to attain the Way. You should ponder this well, and keep far away from all evils. Choose what is good and practice it diligently. Love, desire, splendor, and glory cannot be kept for long; all must be parted with, and none of them brings joy. When you encounter the Buddha in this world, you should strive with diligence. Those who earnestly vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss will gain wisdom and clarity, and merit most excellent. Do not follow your every whim and so betray the sūtras and precepts, falling behind others.”
(The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life)
Question: What does “That land refuses none, yet beings are drawn along by their own natural karma” mean?

Answer: In the sūtra, “That land refuses none, yet beings are drawn along by their own natural karma” means this: the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss does not refuse any sentient being (“that land refuses none”), yet the reason beings cannot be reborn there is that at the hour of death they cannot maintain right mindfulness, the dark states appear before them, and so they are carried by karmic force to be reborn in the six realms, utterly unable to control themselves (“drawn along by their own natural karma”). On this point, Master Lianchi has an extremely important instruction in his Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra, which I now quote and annotate as follows:

[Those who are confused at the hour of death are so because in ordinary times they follow their deluded thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are much scattered. When the time comes to relinquish the warmth of life, all that they have done throughout their lives appears before them; their minds are frightened and terrified, and their movements become disordered. Those who should fall into the hells see mountains of knives and trees of swords as gardens and groves. Those who should fall among the animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey to be a fine hall. Even those who have done good and should be born among humans or devas cannot avoid loving or hating their parents. Even sages of the small vehicle at the initial stage, and bodhisattvas newly resolved on the path, still cannot rightly know their entering and leaving. All of this is what is meant by confusion. Riding on this confusion, within the three realms one undergoes rebirth according to karma among the seven destinies. Now, if one has already attained single-mindedness without confusion, then at the hour of death, inwardly one concentrates right mindfulness and outwardly one evokes the Buddha’s welcome; casting off this present body, one is reborn straightway in that land. As the Buddha said: “To the extent the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.” He also said: “All lands are upheld by thought alone.” When pure thought is perfected, rebirth is assured — of this there is surely no doubt.]

Those who are confused at the hour of death are all so because in ordinary times they follow their deluded thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are much scattered. When the four great elements begin to dissolve, all that one has done throughout one’s life appears before one; the mind is frightened and terrified, and one’s conduct becomes disordered. Those who should fall into the hells take mountains of knives and trees of swords to be beautiful gardens. Those who should fall among the animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey to be a magnificent hall. Even those who have done good and should be born in the human or heavenly realms, upon entering the womb, cannot avoid loving the mother and hating the father (and so be born male), or loving the father and hating the mother (and so be born female). Even those of the small vehicle who have attained the first fruit, and bodhisattvas newly resolved on the path, still have the obscuration of rebirth between lives and cannot rightly know their entering and leaving the womb. All of this is confusion. Because of the confusion at the hour of death, one is reborn according to karma among the seven destinies within the three realms. Now that one has already attained single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation, at the hour of death, inwardly one concentrates right mindfulness and outwardly one evokes the Buddha’s welcome; casting off this present body, one is reborn straightway in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. As the Buddha said: ‘To the extent the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure’ (to the extent the mind is pure, the Buddha-land one is born into is also pure). The Buddha also said: ‘All lands are upheld by thought alone’ (all lands are upheld solely by the mind’s thought). Therefore, when one who recites the Buddha’s name maintains clear right mindfulness at the hour of death and perfects pure thought, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Of this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt.

[Seven destinies] The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, immortals, devas, and asuras. “Destiny” (qù) means the direction toward which one tends. [Buddha-land] The realm taught and transformed by a single Buddha, distinguished into pure lands, defiled lands, reward lands, and Dharma-nature lands.
Question: Then how should Pure Land practitioners ensure their rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the hour of death?
Answer: The condition for rebirth is:
ten recitations at the hour of death — if uninterrupted, rebirth follows.
For details, see
“The Conditions for Rebirth”
. Therefore, in daily life one must practice uninterrupted tenfold recitation until it becomes second nature. For details, see
“Ten Recitations at the Hour of Death — If Uninterrupted, Rebirth Follows”
Question: In the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says: “Easy to go there, yet no one goes.” Since it is easy to go, why is single-mindedness without confusion necessary?

Answer: “Easy” here is said in comparison with other methods. Other methods require one to cut off all afflictions in order to end birth and death and escape the cycle of rebirth, whereas the Pure Land method requires only that one subdue afflictions and recite the Buddha’s name (with single-mindedness without confusion). The difficulty of the two differs as vastly as heaven and earth. Hence Master Yinguang said:
“Had the Tathāgata not opened this method
(had Śākyamuni Buddha not revealed this Pure Land method)
, then not a single sentient being in this Dharma-ending age could end birth and death.”
(Preface to the Verses on the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life)
Question: How can one attain single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation?
Answer: The greatest obstacle to attaining single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation is deluded thought. In the practice textbook
Awareness in Buddha-Recitation

of the “Practice-as-Taught Online Buddhist Academy,” the causes of deluded thought and how to overcome it effectively are analyzed in detail; it also explains in detail the concrete steps and methods of study and practice for attaining single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation. So long as one has true faith and earnest vows, and strives assiduously, advancing step by step and persevering steadily, one is certain to attain single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation.
Appendix: The Wondrous Key to Buddha-Recitation
Chan Master Cao’an

Amitābha Buddha — who cannot recite his name, and yet it is so hard to recite? The Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss — who does not wish to be born there, and yet how few attain birth? The reason is
(it is because)
that those who recite the Buddha’s name have not obtained the key. What makes
(that is, enables)

one’s Buddha-recitation earnest and true — is it not the single word “death”? Keep the word “death” in mind, and circumstances naturally grow cold, and affection naturally grows light. Fame, gain, power, and pride all avail nothing here; what one has seen, heard, and understood becomes useless at that hour. When the four great elements separate, upon what can one rely? A lonely soul with no master — how can it be free? If at that moment one does not see Amitābha, one may well meet a rākṣasa. If one is not born in the Pure Land, one may well enter a donkey’s womb. Even without evil karma, one still cannot avoid coming and going among humans and devas. Even with wholesome causes, one is still vexed that
(alas)
heavenly blessings are so soon exhausted.
[Rākṣasa] A general name for malevolent demons.

Say not that you have your own mastery — drawn by karmic retribution, it is truly hard to escape. Say not that there is no birth and death — while the knowing mind is not exhausted, you remain in the round of rebirth. Do not regard this matter as remote — what tomorrow holds, today you cannot know. Do not take this matter lightly — miss this life, and you sink for endless kalpas. Of all matters, none is greater than the great matter of birth and death; beside it, every other matter is a matter of no urgency. At every moment, regard it as the hour of death, and every moment becomes a moment for Buddha-recitation. To recite the Buddha’s name in this way — this is a heart of earnestness; and only with such an earnest heart can one be born in the Pure Land. One must exert death-serious effort to accomplish the pure karma; only by constantly keeping the hour of death in mind will one be willing to be earnest. This is the stairway to Buddhahood; this is indeed the wondrous key to Buddha-recitation.

[“Of all matters, none is greater than the great matter of birth and death; beside it, every other matter is a matter of no urgency”] No matter whatever compares in gravity with the great matter of birth and death, so no matter is an urgent matter.
